**Time to loss of consciousness **

The effect site in a pharmacokinetic model is a compartment of negligible volume contained within the central compartment. Equilibration between plasma and effect site is modelled by Ke0 - the rate constant for effect site elimination 

t1/2ke0 describes the half time for equilibration 

Time to loss of consciousness is dependent on achieving desired plasma concentration

- Incorporates both the amount of drug reaching the blood brain barrier
- The rate the drug will diffuse across the membrane 

Time to loss of consciousness after IV injection of a drug is dependent on the rate of reaching effective effect site concentration (ce). 

This is a combination of pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic determinants described by the t1/2ke0

- The effect site in a pharmacokinetic model is a compartment of negligible volume contained within the central compartment. 
- Equilibration between plasma and effect site is modelled by Ke0 - the rate constant for effect site elimination 
- t1/2ke0 describes the half time for equilibration 
- Large ke0 (rapid drug flow) → short t1/2Ke0 → more rapid onset

Drugs that have the following properties larger Ke0 (↓t1/2 Keo):

- Low protein binding 
- Low unionised portion
- High lipid solubility 
- Low MW

**Pharmacokinetic determinants of the Ke0 **

**Rate of Plasma Concentration Rise **

- ↑Rate of Administration → more rapid rise in plasma concentration

**Drug available for diffusion across BBB**

- ↑CO → inc VR →↑Rate of delivery to BBB  
- More proximal delivery (CVC) →  ↑ Rate of delivery to BBB
- ↓Ionisation 
- ↓Protein binding 

**Rate of diffusion across the membrane**\
\
Rate of diffusion described by Fick’s law

D=ΔP.A.k/t

ΔP = Concentration gradient. 

- ↑ Concentration in plasma  →↑ more rapid diffusion
- Concentration able to be delivered however is limited by potential toxic side effects.

A=Diffusion/membrane area - unable to be changed in this situation

k = diffusion constant s/(sqMW), rate of diffusion is proportional to the lipid solubility of the drug and inversely related to the MW. ↓MW + ↑Lipid →↑Rate of diffusion 

t = thickness of membrane, relatively unchanged in most clinical situations
